analysis.investment_thesis: Capri Global is a fast-growing NBFC with an impressive 37.2% revenue CAGR and 30.4% net profit CAGR over 9 years, focused on underserved MSME and affordable housing segments in India — structurally attractive lending niches. However, D/E of 2.52x, finance costs compounding at 67.9% CAGR (outpacing revenue), ROE of only 11.8%, and total assets nearly doubling in a single year (₹15K to ₹24K Cr) is the classic fingerprint of a leveraged growth machine where credit quality is the terminal risk.
key_strengths: Revenue CAGR of 37.2% and net profit CAGR of 30.4% over 9 years demonstrates genuine franchise building in underpenetrated MSME and affordable home loan segments — real demand pull, not financial engineering

Promoter holding at 59.92% with DII ownership at 20.09% signals institutional confidence; the equity capital raise that grew equity from ₹3,565 Cr to ₹6,673 Cr in FY25 shows ability to access capital markets
Forward P/E of 12.96x is reasonable for the growth profile; if credit quality holds, the earnings multiple contraction as growth normalises could reward patient investors
key_risks: Finance costs compounding at 67.9% CAGR — materially faster than revenue (37.2%) and net profit (30.4%) — means NIM is structurally compressing; the funding cost treadmill will eventually catch up to the loan yield
Total assets nearly doubled from ₹15,150 Cr to ₹24,413 Cr in a single year (FY25); hyper-rapid loan book expansion in Indian NBFCs has repeatedly preceded asset quality crises (DHFL, IL&FS, SREI)

ROE of 11.8% and ROCE of 11.2% are below Munger's 15% minimum — for a highly leveraged financial business, sub-12% ROE means the equity owner is not being adequately compensated for the credit and liquidity risks embedded in the balance sheet
red_flags: OCF negative in all 5 of the last 5 years, reaching -₹4,312 Cr in FY25 — while normal for a growing NBFC disbursing loans, the absolute scale and acceleration means the business is entirely dependent on continuous external funding; any credit market disruption is existential
P/S of 7.2x is extremely expensive for an NBFC — you are paying ₹7 for every ₹1 of revenue in a business with thin and uncertain net margins; comparable well-established HFCs trade at 2–4x revenue

Gold loan addition alongside MSME and home loans represents business model sprawl — each product has different credit, regulatory, and operational requirements; spreading thin across multiple segments before mastering any is a classic small NBFC mistake
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Capri Global is building real institutional presence in India's massive credit gap for small borrowers — MSME loans, affordable housing, and gold loans collectively address hundreds of millions of underserved customers. The growth statistics are genuine and the promoter group has demonstrated commitment through the large equity infusion. The business model is not fraudulent — it is simply being built very quickly, and speed is the enemy of credit quality in lending. The real test will come when the business cycle turns or when a specific segment (say, affordable housing in a Tier-3 city) experiences stress. The numbers do not yet reflect such a test.

The structural concern I cannot dismiss is the finance cost trajectory — growing at 67.9% CAGR against 37.2% revenue growth means the cost of borrowed money is rising faster than the income from deployed money. This is the ticking clock in every aggressive NBFC. Either the loan yields must expand (unlikely in competitive MSME/housing lending), costs must be contained (hard as leverage rises), or growth must slow. At D/E of 2.52x and assets doubling annually, Capri is running an aggressive leverage experiment. I want to see 2–3 more years of data on NPA trends and NIM sustainability before committing meaningful capital.
